content:
Big release - Open Source Recursive Self Improvement from @hexoai 

Shows AI agent can improve both how it works and what it internally knows after seeing its own task results.
i.e. by repeatedly training on its own task feedback, not by relying on a human to hand-code every strategy.

Most agents today are frozen workers: you can give them better prompts, better tools, better retry rules, and better code, but the actual model usually stays the same. 

SIA (Self Improving AI framework) changes the outer workflow, called the harness, and also changes the model’s weights, which are the internal settings that store learned patterns. which means task feedback changes the model’s internal parameters, pushing it toward domain knowledge.

The paper reports a 56.6% gain on LawBench, 91.9% runtime reduction on GPU kernels, and 502% improvement on single-cell RNA denoising over baseline.

content:
AI agents aren't failing because they're not smart enough.

They're failing because they forget everything.

Every conversation.
Every meeting.
Every decision.
Every relationship.

The entire AI industry is obsessed with making models smarter.

Meanwhile, @garrytan is building something far more important:

Memory.

GBrain isn't another chatbot.
It isn't another RAG wrapper.
It isn't another "AI workspace."

It's a persistent brain for AI.

A system that remembers what happened yesterday, connects it to what happened six months ago, and uses that context to make better decisions tomorrow.

That's a fundamentally different direction.

The most interesting part?

GBrain doesn't just retrieve information.

It synthesizes it.

Instead of:

"Here are 10 notes that might help."

It tells you:

"Here's what matters.
Here's what's unresolved.
Here's what changed.
And here's what the system still doesn't know."

That last part is what caught my attention.

Most AI products optimize for confidence.

GBrain optimizes for context.

Most AI products answer questions.

GBrain tries to build understanding.

And the "dream cycle" concept is wild.

While you sleep, it:

• fixes citations
• merges duplicates
• enriches entities
• updates relationships
• consolidates memory

Almost like memory consolidation in the human brain.

The more I look at this space, the more I think we're watching a major shift:

AI Chatbots → AI Agents → AI Systems With Memory

And the companies that own the memory layer may end up owning the biggest moat of all.

Because intelligence is useful.

But intelligence that remembers compounds.

Curious what you think, @garrytan —

As frontier models become increasingly commoditized, does the long-term moat move from intelligence to memory?

content:
October. is shaping up to be a major milestone for @wardenprotocol and the future of onchain AI agents.

This month isn't just about faster verification. It's about building a trust layer that can scale across the entire agent economy.

Key highlights coming in October:

• settleSwarm goes live on Base Mainnet, enabling hundreds to thousands of micro-verifiers to validate each task.

• Verification speed gets a major upgrade with claim and submit windows optimized for sub 3 minute completion.

• Provider audit dashboards will automatically surface overlap anomalies, making verification more transparent and reliable.

• ERC-8004 Agent Registry launches, giving every agent a persistent onchain identity and portable reputation.

• Reputation based pricing tiers arrive, allowing top performing operators to earn premium rates based on proven track records.

• Public agent search becomes available, making it easier to discover agents, review their history, and verify their receipts.

The bigger vision is what stands out most.

Warden Protocol is pushing agent reputation beyond simple scores and turning it into a first-class onchain asset. As verification scales toward milliseconds per check, trust becomes programmable, portable, and transparent.

The future of autonomous agents needs verifiable reputation, and @wardenprotocol is building exactly that.

title: The deadly Ebola outbreak is proving difficult to control
content: The alert was raised on May 5 . Four health-care workers in the Ituri Province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo had died from an unknown illness within four days. Rapid response teams were sent to investigate, and tests at a research center in Kinshasa revealed the culprit: the Bundibugyo virus, one of the viruses that cause Ebola. Suspected cases of the disease have snowballed in the last few weeks. By May 24, the WHO had estimated that 223 people had died from the disease. There were over 900 suspected cases. Today’s figures are likely to be higher. A couple of weeks ago, I covered the hantavirus outbreak aboard a cruise ship. Three people sadly died, but the outbreak itself was kept under control. There have been no further deaths, and passengers have been safely repatriated. The picture for Ebola is far bleaker. And there are several reasons why. The most obvious is the disease itself. Ebola is a severe disease with an average 50% fatality rate. Previous outbreaks have resulted in thousands of deaths. (Hantavirus also has a high fatality rate, but it doesn’t usually spread as easily between humans.)  Between 2014 and 2016, an Ebola outbreak in West Africa caused more than 11,000 deaths. A more recent outbreak, which took place between 2018 and 2020, caused 2,299 deaths before being brought under control with a vaccination campaign. But those outbreaks were caused by the Zaire virus, which has a different genetic sequence. There is no vaccine for the Bundibugyo virus. We don’t know if the two vaccines approved for Zaire might also work for Bundibugyo. There’s a concern they might even make things worse by interfering with a person’s immune response to the virus.   Scientists are working on potential Bundibugyo vaccines . But the most advanced efforts are still months away from clinical trials. There are no specific antiviral treatments for the virus, either. title: How the Pope’s Magnifica Humanitas offers a template for individuals to meet the AI moment
content: Pope Leo XIV’s new encyclical on artificial intelligence includes a statement that warrants serious attention from technologists and policymakers: “Technology is never neutral.” Magnifica Humanitas (“Magnificent Humanity”) is a clarion call to all people to act with courage and solidarity as we enter an age already being transformed by artificial intelligence, the greatest change in human life since the Industrial Revolution. As the pope says, the choice before us—the choice AI presents—is one between the Tower of Babel and the rebuilding of our common humanity.  In the biblical story of the Tower of Babel, humans sought to build a massive structure that reached all the way to Heaven, only to have their project thwarted when God made those involved unable to understand one another. It was a pursuit fixated on relentless growth, divorced from any concern about God’s commandments or the human cost. It resulted in failure and atomization. The Book of Nehemiah, however, offers a contrasting narrative, in which the rebuilding of Jerusalem after a period of violence and displacement becomes an opportunity for humanity to show its collaborative resilience. As the encyclical puts it, “The city is reborn, not through the initiative of one man, but through the shared responsibility of all: men, women, priests, artisans, heads of households and young people all play a part. It is an undertaking with God at the center, which rebuilds relationships before rebuilding with stones.” Is there any question which road we are currently barreling down? And can there be any doubt which we would do well to walk together?  We are both Catholics, members of religious communities and longtime advocates within the movement for socially responsible investment. content:
Self Improving AI (SIA) beats Karpathy's autoresearcher agent by improving itself!

SIA is a Self Improving AI framework to autonomously improve the performance of any AI system (Model / Agent) on a benchmark task.

Most agent frameworks are static. Fixed harness, fixed model weights, fixed memory layer. They plan, act, and use tools. SIA operates on a different layer entirely.

SIA focuses on one problem: how do you design structured feedback loops that allow an agent to evaluate its own performance, adapt its strategy, and get better over time?

After every run, SIA evaluates itself and improves three things. It updates its own harness. Updates the weights of its underlying model. Updates its own memory layer to handle new complexities. The agent rewrites itself based on what it learned.

On MLE-Bench, OpenAI's benchmark for evaluating an agent's ability to train ML models, SIA climbed to the top of the leaderboard. Beat every specialized ML research agent including MLEvolve and AIRA-dojo. Then kept improving and displaced its own previous versions on the leaderboard.

I've shared the link to the paper and the repo in the replies!

content:
Most people think Prompt Engineering is about finding the perfect prompt.

It's not.

It's about removing ambiguity.

And once you understand that, AI starts feeling a lot less like a chatbot and a lot more like a competent teammate.

The reason most people get average outputs isn't because they're using the wrong model.

It's because they're asking AI to fill in gaps it was never supposed to fill.

Think about it.

If you asked a new employee:

"Make our marketing better."

You wouldn't expect great work.

There are too many unanswered questions.

Better for who?

Which platform?

What's the goal?

Who's the audience?

What does success look like?

Yet that's exactly how most people prompt AI.

They give it a vague objective and hope for a specific result.

The best prompt engineers do the opposite.

They reduce uncertainty.

They tell the model:

→ What they're trying to achieve
→ Why it matters
→ Who it's for
→ What constraints exist
→ What the final output should look like

And suddenly the quality jumps.

Not because the AI became smarter.

Because the instructions became clearer.

That's why prompt engineering isn't really a technical skill.

It's a thinking skill.

The process forces you to answer questions most people skip:

• What exactly am I trying to get done?
• What information is actually relevant?
• What does a good outcome look like?
• What should be included—and excluded?

The clearer those answers become, the better AI performs.

A simple framework:

Goal → Context → Format → Constraints → Iterate

That's the foundation behind almost every high-quality prompt you'll ever write.

No secret prompt packs.

No magic templates.

No "ultimate ChatGPT hack."

Just clarity.

And that's what makes prompt engineering so valuable.

Because the people who learn it aren't just becoming better at using AI.

They're becoming better at communicating, planning, and thinking.

AI simply exposes the difference.

“don’t break this API”

ただのチャート分析ツールではない。

開発元いわく「一人で動かせるウォール街」。AIが市場を調べて、売買プランまで組み立ててくれる。

できることがえぐい。

→ 株・仮想通貨・為替・コモディティまで横断でリサーチ

title: Microsoft、Windows 11「内蔵保護で十分」ブログを静かに削除、業界への配慮か方針転換か
content: Microsoftが4月に公開していた「Windows 11の内蔵保護だけで十分」という趣旨の セキュリティブログ が、5月下旬に予告なく削除されていたことが分かりました。記事はMicrosoft Learning Centerに掲載されていましたが、現在はトップページへリダイレクトされる状態になっています。 削除されたブログの主張とは 問題となったブログは「2026年のベストアンチウイルスはWindowsに内蔵されている保護機能」というタイトルで、Windows 11に標準搭載されている以下のような機能を強調していました。 Microsoft Defender Antivirus SmartScreen Smart App Control ランサムウェア対策機能 など 記事では、多くのユーザーは サードパーティ製アンチウイルスを追加する必要はない と明言しており、これがパートナー企業にとっては刺激的な内容だった可能性があります。例えば以下のような文章が掲載されていました。 Do you still need third‑party antivirus in 2026? For many Windows 11 users, Microsoft Defender Antivirus covers everyday risk without requiring additional software. The choice to add third‑party antivirus depends on how you use your PC and which features you value. When built‑in protection is enough: Windows antivirus protection is usually sufficient when Windows 11 runs with default protections enabled, updates are installed regularly, and software downloads are deliberate. Microsoft Defender Antivirus and SmartScreen already address common threats such as malicious files, phishing sites, and unsafe installers. When additional tools may help: You might consider extra security software if you manage multiple devices, share devices with family members, or want services like identity monitoring or parental controls. Each added tool increases background activity and complexity, so choose tools that match real needs. 2026年にサードパーティ製アンチウイルスはまだ必要？ 多くの Windows 11 ユーザーにとって、Microsoft Defender Antivirus は日常的なリスクに十分対応できるため、追加のソフトを入れる必要はありません。サードパーティ製アンチウイルスを導入するかどうかは、PC の使い方や求める機能によって変わります。 内蔵の保護で十分なケース： Windows 11 の既定の保護機能が有効になっており、更新プログラムを定期的に適用し、ソフトウェアのダウンロードも慎重に行っている場合、標準のウイルス対策でほとんどの状況に対応できます。Microsoft Defender Antivirus と SmartScreen は、悪意あるファイル、フィッシングサイト、危険なインストーラーといった一般的な脅威をすでにカバーしています。 追加ツールが役立つケース： 複数のデバイスを管理している場合や、家族と PC を共有している場合、あるいは ID 監視やペアレンタルコントロールなどの追加サービスが必要な場合は、サードパーティ製のセキュリティソフトを検討してもよいでしょう。 ただし、ツールを増やすほどバックグラウンドの処理やシステムの複雑さも増すため、本当に必要な機能に絞って選ぶことが大切です。 とはいえ、Windows 11の標準保護が日常的な脅威には十分である一方、家族共有や複数デバイス管理、ID監視など追加機能が必要な場合はサー

title: Windows 11のPatch Tuesdayが失敗する問題、KB5089573 で修正完了
content: Windows 11の一部環境で発生していた、「 5月の月例更新プログラムKB5089549がインストールできない 」という不具合について、Microsoftが正式に修正を行ったことがわかりました。 影響を受けていたのはWindows 11 24H2と25H2のユーザーで、更新が35〜36%付近で止まり、エラーコード0x800f0922とともにロールバックされるという厄介な症状が発生していました。エラーメッセージは「Something didn’t go as planned.Undoing changes.」と曖昧で、ユーザーにとっては状況が分かりづらいものでした。 修正方法は「KB5089573」を入れるだけ Microsoftはこの問題をプレビューアップデート KB5089573 で修正してます。KB5089573の ドキュメント には以下のような内容が含まれています。 非セキュリティのプレビュー更新プログラムKB5089573をインストールするだけで問題は解消され、追加の作業は不要とのことです。 Microsoftはすでにこの問題が、EFI System Partition(ESP)の空き容量が10MB以下しかないデバイスで発生することをつきとめ、レジストリ編集やKnown Issue Rollback(KIR)で回避することができると説明していましたが、今回の修正によりこれらの 回避策 が不要になったことは大きな前進といえます。 KB5089573は新機能の宝庫 なお、プレビューアップデートのKB5089573は、単なるバグ修正パッチではありません。Low Latency Profileによるパフォーマンス改善、Shared Audio、タスクマネージャーの強化、Windows Searchの改善など、多数の新機能や改善が含まれています。 プレビュー版を先に適用するか、6月9日のPatch Tuesdayで一般提供されるのを待つかはユーザー次第ですが、今回の不具合に悩まされていた人にとっては、早めに適応しても良いかもしれません。

content:
【速報】
Anthropicの新モデル「Claude Opus 4.8」、
物理シミュレーションでOpus 4.7を明らかに超えてると話題😳これ、何がやばいかというと👇
https://t.co/lFgI8Whndn
同じプロンプトを投げた結果、
Opus 4.8は素のHTML5 Canvasだけで、かなり重い物理現象をそのまま動かしてきた。

やらせたのはこの3つ。
・カオスに揺れるトリプル振り子
・1kgと10万kgのブロック衝突でπの桁を数える実験
・ピン格子を落ちる球がベルカーブに積み上がるガルトンボード

特にヤバいのが、
「πの桁を衝突回数で数えて」
みたいなざっくり指示だけで、

Opus 4.8がCanvas上に物理シミュレーションを構築
↓
ブロックが壁と巨大ブロックの間で跳ねる
↓
衝突回数が3,141…に近づいていく
という挙動まで実装してくるところ。
これ、もはや
「それっぽいアニメーションを作るAI」じゃない。

数式、状態更新、衝突判定、描画、可視化まで含めて、
AIが頭の中で物理現象を組み立てている。
正直、軽い試作なら
Matter.jsやThree.jsを呼ぶ前に、
まずAIに物理エンジンごと書かせる時代に入りつつある。
AIを「コードを書く相棒」として使う段階から、
“現象そのものを実装する計算屋”として使う段階へ。

で、
「Claude Code進化早すぎて、正直ついていけてない…」
って感じてる人へ。
その感覚、かなり正常です。
ここ最近だけでも、
・/simplify → /code-review
・Plugins
・権限管理まわり
・レビュー設計
・Hooks
・Subagents

とか、思想レベルでかなり変わってきてる。

ただ、この変化についていけるかで、
半年後の生産性かなり変わると思う。

content:
Most people think AI coding gets better when models get smarter.

I think that's becoming false.

Claude Opus 4.6 already knows how to write code.

The real bottleneck is whether it can understand a massive codebase efficiently.

That's a completely different problem.

Take VS Code.

~2.45 million lines of code.
5,300+ files.
55,000+ indexed chunks.

Most AI agents explore repositories like this:

grep

open file

grep again

open another file

repeat

They're not reasoning.

They're searching.

And search becomes the bottleneck.

That's why this benchmark caught my attention.

SocratiCode ran a head-to-head test on the VS Code codebase with Claude Opus 4.6.

Results:

• 61.5% less context consumed
• 84% fewer tool calls
• 37.2× faster exploration

Not because the model became smarter.

Because the model found the right information faster.

That's the shift most people are missing.

The next generation of AI infrastructure won't just be better models.

It will be better context systems.

Context graphs.
Codebase intelligence engines.
Semantic retrieval.
Dependency mapping.
Knowledge layers.

Because an AI can't reason about code it never sees.

And as repositories grow from thousands of files to millions of lines, context retrieval becomes more important than model intelligence.

The companies solving this problem may end up more valuable than the companies shipping the next benchmark-winning model.

The future of AI coding isn't:

"How smart is Claude?"

It's:

"Can Claude understand your entire codebase before the context window runs out?"

That's where the real race has started.

Open Source.
2.8k+ GitHub stars.

One of the most interesting AI infrastructure projects I've seen recently.
